title: Precedence Graph
description: Build conflict-edge ledgers, detect two- and three-transaction cycles, derive serial witnesses, and distinguish precedence graphs from deadlock wait-for graphs.

questions.question_text: How is an edge added to a precedence graph?
options: One edge per transaction, regardless of conflicts
A directed edge Ti → Tj is added whenever Ti has an operation that conflicts with, and precedes, an operation of Tj on the same data item
An edge is added for every pair of transactions, whether or not they conflict
Edges are added only for COMMIT operations
questions.explanation: Edges represent conflict-based ordering requirements: Ti→Tj means some conflicting operation of Ti had to happen before Tj's corresponding operation.

questions.question_text: What is the precedence graph theorem for conflict serializability?
options: A schedule is conflict-serializable if and only if its precedence graph has no cycles
A schedule is conflict-serializable if and only if its precedence graph has at least one cycle
A schedule is always conflict-serializable regardless of the graph's shape
The precedence graph determines view serializability, not conflict serializability
questions.explanation: This is the fundamental theorem: acyclic precedence graph implies conflict-serializable (with a topological sort giving the equivalent serial order); any cycle implies it is not.

questions.question_text: In Worked Example 1 (schedule S1), why did every single conflicting pair produce an edge in the same direction (T1→T2)?
options: Because T1 and T2 never actually conflict
Because in S1, all of T1's operations on both A and B happen to occur before the corresponding conflicting operations of T2 that touch the same items
Because the graph algorithm forces all edges to point the same way
Because T1 committed before T2 started
questions.explanation: Tracing S1's timeline shows T1's reads/writes on A and B consistently precede T2's conflicting operations on those same items, so every conflict contributes a T1→T2 edge, never the reverse.

questions.question_text: In Worked Example 2 (schedule S2), what specifically causes the precedence graph to contain a cycle?
options: R2(B) precedes W1(B) (giving T2→T1) while R1(A) precedes W2(A) (giving T1→T2), producing edges in both directions between the same two nodes
S2 has more than two transactions
Neither transaction ever writes any data
The schedule includes a blind write
questions.explanation: The two conflicts impose contradictory ordering requirements (T2 before T1 on B, T1 before T2 on A), which manifests as a 2-node cycle in the graph.

questions.question_text: If a precedence graph is acyclic (a DAG) with multiple valid topological sorts, what does that mean?
options: The schedule is not conflict-serializable
More than one serial schedule is equivalent to the given schedule — any of the valid topological orders works
The schedule must be re-executed
Only the alphabetically-first order is valid
questions.explanation: A DAG can admit multiple topological sorts when it isn't a total order; each one represents an equally valid equivalent serial schedule.

questions.question_text: What happens to a precedence graph when two transactions share no conflicting operations at all?
options: The graph is undefined
No edge is drawn between them; if this holds for all pairs, the graph is trivially acyclic and every interleaving is conflict-serializable
An edge is drawn in both directions by default
The schedule is automatically non-serializable
questions.explanation: With zero conflicts, there is no ordering constraint between the transactions, so the graph has no edges connecting them and remains (or stays) acyclic.

questions.question_text: Why does the precedence graph test conflict serializability specifically, rather than view serializability?
options: It preserves all ordered conflicts, including blind write-write order; view equivalence can permit some changes to that order while preserving reads and final writers
It encodes only elapsed time
Blind writes never conflict
It requires all transactions to be read-only
questions.explanation: Blind writes to the same item do conflict. The distinction is that view equivalence preserves a different, sometimes weaker set of relationships, not that the conflict graph ignores write-write pairs.

questions.question_text: Why is the precedence-graph approach preferred over manually searching for a valid sequence of swaps to test conflict serializability?
options: It always gives a different answer than the swap method
Cycle detection in a directed graph is an efficient, well-known algorithm, making it far more practical than exhaustively searching for a swap sequence
Swaps are mathematically undefined
It requires fewer transactions
questions.explanation: Both methods are provably equivalent in their verdict, but cycle detection is computationally efficient and systematic, unlike manually trying every possible reordering.

questions.question_text: What does a precedence-graph vertex represent?
options: A transaction
A table column only
A client window
A backup file
questions.explanation: The graph orders transactions through conflicts among their operations.

questions.question_text: Which pair creates no conflict edge?
questions.explanation: Two reads do not alter the item or each other’s observed value.

questions.question_text: Does overlap alone create an edge?
options: Yes, every overlap creates two
No
Only if a table is large
Only before COMMIT
questions.explanation: An edge needs an ordered conflicting pair on the same item.

questions.question_text: Do blind writes to the same item conflict?
options: No, no reader observes them
Only when the values differ
Yes
Only for text
questions.explanation: Write-write chronology is part of conflict equivalence.

questions.question_text: What does a topological order supply?
options: A guarantee of no business bugs
A backup restore plan
A list of SQL column names
A conflict-equivalent serial witness
questions.explanation: Acyclic precedence constraints can be satisfied by that transaction order.

questions.question_text: Can an acyclic graph have several valid serial witnesses?
options: Yes
No, one is mandatory
Only if no transaction writes
Only with three items
questions.explanation: Independent vertices can be placed in more than one eligible position.

questions.question_text: Why is checking only opposite pairs insufficient?
options: Every graph is automatically acyclic
A cycle can involve three or more transactions
Only two transactions can conflict
It proves deadlock freedom
questions.explanation: A directed triangle can have no opposite pair and still be cyclic.

questions.question_text: Does deleting an unrelated read remove the A/B/C cycle?
options: Yes, every shorter history is serializable
Only if the read has a long name
No
Only after sorting vertices
questions.explanation: Actual cycle dependencies must change.

questions.question_text: What does an arrow in a wait-for graph mean?
options: Always an earlier read-write conflict
A column rename
A committed backup
A current wait on another transaction’s resource
questions.explanation: Wait-for and precedence graphs encode different relations.

questions.question_text: Does an acyclic precedence graph rule out dirty reads?
options: No
Yes, universally
Only for numeric items
Only if there are two vertices
questions.explanation: Recovery and visibility constraints require their own analysis.

questions.question_text: The only edge is T1→T3. May T2 precede both?
options: No, T2 always follows T3
Yes
Only if T2 aborts
Only if A is NULL
questions.explanation: T2 has no precedence constraint in the stated graph.

questions.question_text: What is a complete negative conflict-serializability proof?
options: A matching final balance
A slow query alone
A justified directed cycle in the complete graph
A nonalphabetical vertex order
questions.explanation: A cycle imposes incompatible serial-order requirements.

notes:
## Turn conflicting operation order into a graph

A precedence graph represents the ordering constraints that a read/write schedule imposes between transactions. Each transaction is a vertex. A directed edge from Ti to Tj means an operation of Ti occurred before a conflicting operation of Tj. In the classical single-version item model, the schedule is conflict serializable exactly when this graph is acyclic. A topological ordering of an acyclic graph supplies a conflict-equivalent serial transaction order.

The graph is evidence about one specified history, not an image of every lock wait or a guarantee about arbitrary SQL execution. Define the logical data items and preserve each transaction's program order. Write r1(A) for T1 reading A and w2(B) for T2 writing B. Reads and writes can be abstract operations derived from larger application statements, so state the abstraction before classifying the result.

## Add an edge only for a genuine conflict

Two operations conflict when they belong to different transactions, access the same item and at least one writes. Read-read pairs do not create edges. Writes to different items do not create edges in this simplified model. Operations inside one transaction also do not produce intertransaction graph edges, although their internal order must remain intact in any compared execution.

For each item, list the operations in their schedule order. Compare earlier and later operations from different transactions and add the appropriate directed edge when they conflict. Retain an edge ledger with the item and the two operations justifying each arrow. Repeated evidence for the same edge does not require several graph arrows, but keeping the evidence helps another reader check that no dependency was omitted.

| Earlier operation | Later operation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| r1(A) | r2(A) | No edge |
| r1(A) | w2(A) | T1→T2 |
| w1(A) | r2(A) | T1→T2 |
| w1(A) | w2(A) | T1→T2 |
| w1(A) | w2(B) | No edge for distinct items |

Do not create an edge merely because two transactions overlap in time or their names appear next to one another. Conversely, do not omit an edge because neither transaction read the other's write. Write-write order is itself a conflict constraint, including blind writes whose intermediate values no transaction observes. The graph preserves more than the read-from relationships used by view equivalence.

## Work through a one-direction example

Let S1 be r1(A), w1(A), r2(A), w2(A), r1(B), w1(B), r2(B), w2(B). On A, T1's operations precede the conflicting T2 operations. On B, the same direction holds. The graph therefore has T1→T2 and no reverse edge. Although T2 begins its A work before T1 finishes its B work, the interleaving preserves the same conflict order as serial T1 followed by T2.

A topological ordering is T1, T2. This is a witness of conflict serializability, not a claim that the original list was physically serial. Adjacent exchanges of nonconflicting operations from different transactions can move T1's B operations across T2's A operations without changing the required conflict order. The graph summarizes those constraints without requiring an exhaustive search over swap sequences.

## Find the two-direction contradiction

Let S2 be r1(A), r2(B), w1(B), w2(A). The earlier r1(A) and later w2(A) give T1→T2. The earlier r2(B) and later w1(B) give T2→T1. The graph has a directed cycle. No serial order can place T1 both before and after T2, so this history is not conflict serializable in the stated model.

The verdict does not depend on choosing numeric values that visibly produce a bad total. A particular fixture can coincidentally end with the same values as a serial execution while its conflict relationships still disagree. The property concerns every preserved conflicting-operation order, not only the final numbers in one run. Keep arithmetic checks and structural equivalence checks as separate evidence.

## Use topological sorting for a positive proof

One topological-sorting method repeatedly selects a vertex with no incoming edges, outputs it and removes its outgoing edges. If all vertices are output, the graph is acyclic and that sequence is a valid serial witness. If vertices remain but none has zero indegree, a cycle prevents completion. The method also makes independent choices visible when several vertices are eligible at the same step.

Suppose the only edge is T1→T3 and T2 is independent. Valid orders include T1, T2, T3; T2, T1, T3; and T1, T3, T2. T3 cannot precede T1, but T2 can occupy several positions. Multiple topological orders mean the history is conflict equivalent to several serial orders, not that the graph failed to decide its property. A positive proof needs one valid order; a cycle proves none exists.

## Check cycles involving more than two transactions

Not every failure appears as two opposite arrows between one pair. Edges T1→T2, T2→T3 and T3→T1 form a three-transaction cycle even when there is no reverse edge for any individual pair. Checking only whether two transactions point at each other misses this case. Use a complete cycle-detection or topological-sort argument rather than a visual shortcut that inspects only adjacent vertices.

For a concrete history, use w1(A), r2(A), w2(B), r3(B), w3(C), r1(C), with each transaction's listed order preserved. A gives T1→T2, B gives T2→T3 and C gives T3→T1. All three arrows survive if an unrelated read of D is removed. Repairing the cycle requires a different admitted operation order or concurrency mechanism that changes an actual cycle dependency, followed by a new analysis.

## Distinguish precedence graphs from wait-for graphs

A wait-for graph represents transactions currently waiting on resources held by others. Its cycles can indicate a deadlock under the relevant resource model. A precedence graph instead represents the order of conflicting accesses in a history. Its cycle indicates failure of conflict serializability. The diagrams can use the same transaction names while their edges have different meanings and different construction rules.

An acyclic precedence graph does not prove deadlock freedom for the protocol that attempted to execute a workload. Likewise, a successful deadlock recovery does not prove that every admitted completed history meets the intended serializability property. Ask whether an arrow means earlier conflicting access or a current wait before interpreting any graph found in a monitoring screen or textbook exercise.

## Keep recovery and richer SQL behavior separate

The schedule w1(A), r2(A), c1, c2 has only T1→T2 in its conflict graph, yet T2 read an uncommitted value before c1. Conflict serializability therefore does not by itself guarantee cascadelessness or strictness. A dependent commit before the source commit can raise a separate recoverability problem. Include commit and abort markers when those properties are part of the question.

View serializability can admit some blind-write histories with cyclic conflict graphs because it preserves read sources and final writers rather than all conflict order. Blind write-write pairs still create graph edges; they are not nonconflicting operations. Real SQL adds predicate reads, multiple versions and statement-specific behavior. A row-only diagram that omits a relevant predicate dependency cannot justify the full application's concurrency contract.

Retain the exact schedule beside the graph so reviewers can recompute every arrow. A diagram without its operation ledger can hide an omitted write or an incorrectly reversed edge, even when the final drawing looks tidy.

## Solve two complete graph exercises

First exercise: classify r1(A), r2(A), w2(B), w1(C). The shared A operations are reads, and the writes target distinct items. There are no cross-transaction conflicts, so the two vertices are isolated and either serial order works. The original list remains nonserial if the operations interleave; the graph establishes equivalence rather than literal execution adjacency.

Second exercise: build the ledger for the three-transaction A/B/C history and attempt topological sorting. Every vertex has an incoming edge, so no first vertex can be chosen. The resulting cycle rules out a conflict-equivalent serial order. Continue with [conflict serializability](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/conflict-serializability), [view serializability](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/view-serializability) and [locking protocols](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/locking-protocol-lab) to connect each graph with the exact property it can prove.
